title: Regulation of proton transference for stable and efficient reactive capture of CO2 from air - Nature Energy
gist: Northwestern/Caltech-led Nature Energy paper (abstract-only preview) argues that electrified reactive CO2 capture fails because of proton mismanagement across the membrane, introduces the proton transference number (tH+) as a design descriptor, and shows that swapping anodic oxygen evolution for gas-fed hydrogen oxidation keeps tH+≈1, delivering 1,000 h stable operation at ~1 V and 100 mA cm−2 and CO from air at 22 GJ t−1 versus >35 GJ t−1 for conventional DAC-plus-electrosynthesis.

insights.claim: Conventional direct air capture combined with electrosynthesis carries an end-to-end energy burden exceeding 35 GJ per tonne of CO, driven largely by the intense heat needed to release tightly bound CO2 from capture liquids.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Thermal regeneration is the cost wall for air-to-fuels; any route that removes it attacks the dominant energy line item in e-fuel/DAC economics.
insights.quote: the resulting end-to-end energy burden exceeds 35 GJ per tonne of CO

insights.claim: Electrified reactive capture, which feeds the CO2 capture liquid directly into an electrolyser, avoids thermal regeneration, but previously reported systems remain energy-intensive and typically fail within 100 hours of operation.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Durability under 100 h has kept reactive capture a lab curiosity; track whether lifetimes move toward the thousands of hours needed for commercial stacks.
insights.quote: yet reported systems remain energy-intensive and typically fail within 100 h

insights.claim: Failures of electrified reactive CO2 capture trace to proton flux across the membrane: too many protons acidify the cathode and degrade the catalyst, while too few starve the proton-driven in situ CO2 release, and both regimes favour parasitic hydrogen evolution.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Reframes the durability problem from catalyst chemistry to ion-transport engineering, pointing value toward membrane and cell-architecture IP rather than new catalysts alone.
insights.quote: these failures trace to proton management

insights.claim: The proton transference number (tH+), defined as the fraction of ionic current carried by protons, is proposed as a quantitative descriptor linking ion transport to CO selectivity, carbon utilization and durability in reactive-capture electrolysers.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: A single measurable design metric lets developers screen membranes and anode chemistries quickly; watch for tH+ appearing in competitor and startup performance claims.

insights.claim: Replacing the oxygen evolution reaction with gas-fed hydrogen oxidation at the anode maintains a proton transference number near 1, enabling 1,000 hours of stable bicarbonate reactive-capture operation at about 1 V and 100 mA cm−2.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: A 10x lifetime jump over the ~100 h norm at ~1 V cell voltage is a material de-risking step for electrochemical CO2-to-CO; the trade-off is that the cell now consumes hydrogen as an input.
insights.quote: enabling 1,000 h of stable operation at ~1 V and 100 mA cm−2

insights.claim: The hydrogen-oxidation-anode reactive capture system produced CO from air-capture solutions at 22 GJ per tonne with greater than 90% carbon utilization while simultaneously regenerating the capture medium.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: 22 GJ/t versus >35 GJ/t for DAC-plus-electrosynthesis is a ~37% energy cut, improving the outlook for air-derived syngas/e-fuels if hydrogen supply cost is acceptable.
insights.quote: CO production from air at 22 GJ t−1 with >90% carbon utilization

insights.claim: The CO2 reactive-capture work was led by Edward H. Sargent's group at Northwestern University with Caltech's William A. Goddard III, funded partly by the US Air Force (agreement FA8650-21-2-5028), BioMADE and the DOE Liquid Sunlight Alliance, and includes an environmental and economic assessment by Jennifer B. Dunn using Argonne's GREET model.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: US defence funding signals interest in on-site air-to-fuel production; techno-economic and life-cycle analysis alongside lab results suggests a push toward commercial relevance.
